strengths: Extends function vectors (FVs) from language-only transformers to large multimodal models (LMMs), targeting spatial relations, which is a relatively unexplored and potentially useful direction.

Uses causal mediation analysis (Average Indirect Effect) to identify causally influential attention heads for relational tasks, and provides heatmaps plus ablations on injection layer, head-set size, and context size.
Shows that extracted FVs can be injected in zero-shot prompts and improve over zero-shot and 4-shot ICL baselines on both synthetic and GQA datasets, at least relatively.
Demonstrates that fine-tuning only the FV while keeping the LMM frozen can improve relational prediction, suggesting a parameter-efficient control mechanism.
Proposes composite FVs for one-shot analogy problems involving untrained spatial relations, providing initial evidence for linear combination/generalization.
Includes ethics and reproducibility statements and promises code/datasets via an anonymous OSF repository.
A limitations section acknowledges the single-model scope, limited relation set, and need for broader evaluation.
weaknesses: Absolute accuracy is low and often at or below chance. In the synthetic task, each image contains one query object, four relational objects, and one distractor, so chance among candidate answers is roughly 20%. Fine-tuned FV accuracy is about 27% (above), 26% (below), 19.5% (left), and 20% (right), meaning left/right performance is essentially chance. The composite FV analogy result is 16.8%, below the ~20% chance level for the synthetic analogy task. This substantially weakens the central claim of meaningful relational reasoning.
The paper repeatedly claims that fine-tuned FVs 'significantly outperform' baselines, but no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported.

GQA results are not adequately reported. The text states Figure 5 contains 7 relations for GQA, but the visible figure shows only 4 synthetic relations and no GQA numbers. Additionally, the GQA training set (101 images) is used for both FV extraction and fine-tuning, with no separate held-out fine-tuning split, raising concerns about overfitting or leakage.
Only one model (OpenFlamingo-4B) and a small set of spatial relations are studied. It remains unclear whether the findings generalize to larger LMMs, other architectures, or non-spatial relations.

Methodological details are insufficient for reproducibility: the token position used to extract attention-head activations, the exact definition of attention-head activations, the token position for AIE replacement, prompt formatting details, and the precise GQA extraction/fine-tuning splits are not fully specified.

The composite FV method is ad hoc: weights are derived from the model's own probabilities rather than learned or theoretically justified, and there is no analysis of why linear combination should capture novel relations. The reported improvement is small and may not exceed chance.

The comparison to in-context learning is not apples-to-apples. Fine-tuned FVs use many training examples (1000 synthetic examples or 101 GQA images with 200 tasks per relation), whereas ICL uses only 4 demonstrations at inference. No comparison to prompt tuning or other parameter-efficient fine-tuning with similar data is provided.

Presentation quality is weak: numerous typos ('MOELS', 'mul timodal', 'illusation', 'lable', 'relation-secific'), inconsistent reference formatting (e.g., Anthropic appears under Alayrac et al. [2025]), and missing or unclear figure details reduce readability and trust.
Evaluation uses top-1 accuracy for the first token of the object label, which may not reflect full label accuracy and can be misleading for multi-token object names.
The limitations discussion does not acknowledge the low absolute performance, chance-level results for horizontal relations, or the potential overlap between GQA extraction and fine-tuning data.
The synthetic task may be solvable through simple positional heuristics, so it is unclear whether the extracted FVs encode relational knowledge or primarily positional biases.
The central claim that FVs 'embed intended relational knowledge and can causally trigger task execution' is not strongly supported given the low and inconsistent accuracy across relations.

strengths: Reasonable and timely research direction: extending the function-vector (FV) framework from language-only transformers to a vision-language model (OpenFlamingo-4B) for spatial relations is a natural and under-explored extension, and the causal-mediation (AIE) analysis identifying a sparse set of intermediate-layer attention heads is a plausible interpretability finding (Figs. 4, 7, 8).

The paper includes a systematic set of ablations (injection layer, head-set size, context size) that probe how the intervention behaves, and reports the non-monotonic dependence on head-set size (peak at 6-12 heads), which is a useful methodological detail.
Reproducibility is comparatively strong: detailed dataset-construction criteria in the supplement (A.1), an explicit ethics statement, and a stated anonymous OSF repository with code and data.
The limitations section is honest about single-architecture scope and the narrow set of relations, and the authors do not hide that the generalization results rest on synthetic data.
weaknesses: The headline claim that fine-tuned function vectors 'significantly outperform in-context learning baselines' rests on an unfair comparison: the fine-tuned FV is optimized on 1,000 labeled zero-shot examples (synthetic) or ~800 relation instances (GQA), whereas the ICL baselines use 4 demonstrations. Supervised optimization over hundreds/thousands of labeled examples beating 4-shot ICL is largely expected and does not by itself demonstrate anything special about function vectors.

Absolute accuracy is very low throughout (fine-tuned FV roughly 20-27% on synthetic; composite FV 16.8% vs 8.3% one-shot), and no random/chance baseline or human ceiling is reported. Because the synthetic images contain only ~5 candidate objects per query, it is unclear whether these numbers are meaningfully above chance, which makes it impossible to judge the practical significance of the gains.

The paper repeatedly claims results 'significantly outperform' baselines but reports no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests; given the small test sets (e.g., 100 GQA images; 101 training images) and small effect sizes, the significance claims are unsupported.

The core interpretability claim is undercut by the paper's own data: the *initial* (untrained) function vector often does not beat 4-shot ICL (e.g., below/left/right in Fig. 5b), so the evidence that the extracted vector alone causally encodes relational knowledge sufficient to 'trigger task execution' is weak; the gains appear only after supervised fine-tuning.

Generalization is demonstrated only on the synthetic analogy task. The abstract and introduction promise 'strong generalization ability,' but the conclusion itself concedes 'these results are based on synthetic images,' i.e., a proof of concept; the abstract overstates the evidence.

Presentation and internal consistency problems: the function vector is defined as a *sum* of mean activations in Eq. 2 but described in the text as *averaging*; the Fig. 4 caption ('right of') conflicts with the text ('left of'); multiple typos and truncated sentences ('Moels' in a section header, 'mul...', 'analog...', 'lable', 'relation-secific', 'illustation'); and malformed/duplicated reference entries (e.g., 'Alayrac et al. [2025] Anthropic').

The composite-vector procedure is potentially circular: the weights w_t are derived from the model's own probabilities under each relation vector, and the resulting composite is then evaluated by the same model, so it is unclear how much the improvement reflects genuine relational composition versus re-weighting the model's own prior.

Fine-tuning a single injected vector while freezing the model is essentially learning a steering vector / soft prompt; framed as such, the 'fine-tuning function vectors' contribution is incremental, and its novelty relative to existing activation-steering and task-vector work (Hojel et al., Huang et al.) is not clearly established.

Evidence is limited to one small model (OpenFlamingo-4B) and a very small real-image subset (101 training images, 201 total), so the generality of the claimed modularity is untested even within the paper's own scope.

strengths: Extends function vectors from LLMs to large multimodal models, providing a novel mechanistic-interpretability angle for spatial relational reasoning in vision-language models.
Uses causal mediation analysis and average indirect effect (AIE) to identify a sparse set of causally influential attention heads, connecting the method to prior LLM work on function vectors.
Evaluates the approach on both a controlled synthetic dataset and the real-image GQA dataset, with ablations on injection layer, head-set size, and context size.

Shows that fine-tuned relation-specific function vectors substantially improve over zero-shot and 4-shot ICL baselines in the reported synthetic setting, and that composite function vectors improve one-shot analogy performance over ICL.
Includes a reproducibility statement, detailed supplementary dataset descriptions, and an ethics statement; code and data are said to be available via an anonymous repository.
weaknesses: The paper repeatedly claims that results are 'significant' but provides no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, making the strength of the improvements uncertain, especially on the small GQA test set (100 images / 200 tasks per relation).

The fine-tuned function-vector comparison to 4-shot ICL is not data- or compute-matched: the vector is trained on 1000 zero-shot examples for synthetic data (or 101 training images for GQA), while ICL uses only four demonstrations. Comparisons to other parameter-efficient adaptation methods under the same data budget are missing.

Absolute accuracies remain low (e.g., 16.8% for composite-function-vector analogy problems; roughly 20–27% for fine-tuned vectors on synthetic relations), which weakens claims about practically 'enhancing control' over relational reasoning.

Methodological details are unclear in key places: it is not specified whether the targeted attention heads are self-attention or cross-attention heads, how head activations from different layers are summed into one vector and then injected at a single layer, or exactly how the AIE is computed for perturbed prompts.

The composite function-vector experiments lack ablations (e.g., uniform weights, random weights, oracle relation weights) and do not directly verify that linear combinations encode novel diagonal relations; the improvement over ICL is small in absolute terms.

The study is limited to OpenFlamingo-4B and a small set of spatial relations, so generalization to larger LMMs and broader relational categories remains untested; the authors acknowledge this but the evidence for modularity is therefore narrow.
Presentation has multiple typos and reference issues (e.g., 'Moels', 'lable', 'rel-secific', inconsistent reference formatting), reducing overall polish.

strengths: The paper extends function-vector analysis from LLMs to LMMs for visual relations, a novel and timely direction in multimodal mechanistic interpretability.
The pipeline is systematic: causal mediation analysis (AIE) identifies candidate attention heads, FVs are extracted, injected zero-shot, fine-tuned, and composed for analogy tasks.
Experiments cover two LMMs (OpenFlamingo, Qwen3-VL) and two datasets (synthetic, GQA) with spatial and agentic relations, plus ablations on injection layer, head-set size, and context size.

Fine-tuned FVs show strong gains for Qwen3-VL on synthetic data (e.g., 72.2% with novel objects vs 21.3% ICL), and composite FVs provide a proof-of-concept for linear composition to untrained compound relations.
The limitations and broader impact are discussed, and the authors claim code is publicly available.
weaknesses: The comparison to in-context learning is not apples-to-apples: fine-tuned FVs are optimized on 1000 labeled examples (or 2,113 GQA training images), while ICL baselines use only 4 demonstrations; no equally supervised baselines (e.g., linear probe, prompt tuning, full fine-tuning) are reported.
The causal claims lack essential controls: no random-vector or random-head injection baselines, so improvements could reflect generic perturbation effects rather than relation-specific encoding.
No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided; several reported differences (e.g., OpenFlamingo synthetic 13.6% vs 11% vs 9.4%) may be within noise.

Absolute accuracy remains low in several settings (e.g., OpenFlamingo synthetic FFV 13.6%, CFV 16.8%), and initial FVs sometimes do not outperform 4-shot ICL (e.g., GQA Spatial Qwen3-VL), limiting the strength of the central claims.
The AIE-based head selection is not validated for necessity/sufficiency (e.g., no knockout of top heads, no comparison to random heads), so the identified subnetwork may be confounded.

The composite-FV analogy evaluation also uses a source example plus FVs extracted from large labeled sets; the one-shot comparison to ICL is therefore not a clean test of compositional generalization.
Reproducibility is incomplete: no code URL, no random seeds, ambiguous per-relation data splits, and some notation inconsistencies (CIE vs. AIE, a_{lj} vs. a_{tj}).
Presentation could be improved: some figure panels/captions are unclear, main text reports averaged results while per-relation details are in the appendix, and claims sometimes exceed the evidence.

strengths: Extends the function-vector framework from LLMs to LMMs for visual relational reasoning, an underexplored direction, and evaluates two different LMMs (OpenFlamingo-4B and Qwen3-VL-4B) on synthetic and GQA-based datasets.

Combines causal mediation analysis, activation patching, zero-shot vector injection, vector fine-tuning, and compositional vector combination in a coherent pipeline, with useful ablation studies on injection layer, number of heads, and context size.

Reports some promising results: fine-tuned relation vectors improve over baselines on several synthetic and GQA tasks, including a novel-object synthetic test, and composite vectors improve one-shot analogy performance over ICL in the reported experiments.
Includes an ethics/impact statement and a limitations section that acknowledges the narrow relation set and the reliance on contextual demonstrations for composite vectors.
weaknesses: The central claim that the extracted vectors are relation-specific is undermined by Appendix G: OpenFlamingo's function vectors for above, below, left, and right have pairwise cosine similarities above 0.9, so they are nearly collinear and cannot encode distinct relational content. The paper reports this but never reconciles it with the main claim or with the composite-vector method.

The main accuracy gains come from fine-tuning a vector on 1000 labeled examples (or 2,113 GQA training images), not from the extracted function vectors. The initial FVs often underperform 4-shot ICL (e.g., Qwen3-VL synthetic initial FV ~21% vs. 4-shot ~27%; GQA Spatial initial FV ~24% vs. 4-shot ~32%), so the evidence that extracted FVs improve zero-shot accuracy is weak.

The comparison to ICL is not apples-to-apples: fine-tuned FVs use gradient training on 1000 examples while ICL uses only four demonstrations at inference. There is no comparison to a linear probe, prompt tuning, or any other method trained on the same amount of data, so the source of the improvement is unclear.

No statistical rigor: figures report single accuracy bars without error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds. Many differences (e.g., GQA agentic where FFV and 4-shot ICL appear similar) may be noise, so the claimed outperformance is not established.

Mechanistic-interpretability claims lack controls. The AIE analysis selects top heads per relation but never compares against random heads, unrelated control tasks, or head ablations, and never quantifies head specificity. The heatmaps are qualitative, so the conclusion that a sparse set of heads encodes visual relations is not adequately supported.

Experimental details are inconsistent or incomplete. Section 4.3 says the GQA Agentic test set contains 1,413 images, but Appendix A.2 says 1,413 is the total agentic set and the test split is 706 images. The chosen injection layers (19 for synthetic, 8 for GQA) are not justified, no layer ablation is shown for GQA, and using the same layer numbers for two architecturally different LMMs is questionable.

The paper does not compare against prior visual or multimodal task-vector methods (e.g., Hojel et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024) even though it cites them and claims to extend that line of work. This makes the novelty and relative benefit of the proposed approach unclear.

The composite-vector analogy task is limited: the 'novel' relations (above-left, above-right, etc.) are simple conjunctions of the four trained spatial relations, tested only on the synthetic dataset. The method requires a source example to infer weights and assumes the target relation lies in the span of the base relations, so the generalization claim is overstated.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper states code is on GitHub but gives no URL; object lists, exact prompts, validation procedures, hyperparameter searches, and model-layer mappings are not fully specified. The manuscript also contains citation-year errors and typos (e.g., 'Qwen3-VL4B-instruct', Awadalla et al. 2025 for a 2023 paper), indicating insufficient care.

The limitations discussion omits the most serious issues: the near-collinear OpenFlamingo FVs, the fine-tuning confound, the lack of statistical tests, and the missing controls in the causal mediation analysis.

strengths: The paper makes a useful and original extension of function vectors from LLMs to large multimodal models, targeting visual relational reasoning. It connects causal mediation analysis with inference-time interventions in a way that is well motivated and timely for multimodal interpretability.

The method is clearly structured: AIE-based attention-head selection, relation-specific function-vector extraction, zero-shot injection, fine-tuning of only the vector, and composite vectors for one-shot analogy tasks. The ablations over injection layer, head-set size, and context size strengthen the empirical picture.

Experiments cover two different LMMs (OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL) and both synthetic and real-image GQA data, including spatial and agentic relations. The use of held-out object and relation generalization tests, plus cross-dataset transfer, is a meaningful effort toward testing generality.

The reported results support the central claim that localized internal representations can be extracted and manipulated: fine-tuned function vectors outperform zero-shot baselines and often 4-shot ICL, and composite function vectors improve one-shot analogy performance on untrained relations.

The paper includes an explicit limitations section and an impact statement, acknowledging the narrow relation set and the dependence of composite vectors on contextual examples. These are appropriate and do not undermine the contribution by themselves.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. Many claims of 'significant' improvement are made without confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple-seed analysis, and several gains are small in absolute terms (e.g., OpenFlamingo novel-object accuracy 13.6% vs. 9.4% ICL; GQA spatial accuracies remain low).

The baselines are incomplete for the fine-tuning claim. Fine-tuned function vectors are trained on 1,000+ examples but are compared mainly to zero-shot and few-shot ICL, not to supervised linear probes, LoRA/PEFT, prompt tuning, or other activation-steering methods trained with the same data. This makes it unclear whether the benefit comes from the function-vector parameterization or simply from supervised adaptation.

Causal specificity is not fully established. The paper shows sufficiency interventions (injecting selected vectors) but does not systematically show necessity or wrong-relation controls: e.g., does injecting the 'above' vector hurt 'below' queries? Does ablating the selected heads damage normal ICL performance? The very high cosine similarity among OpenFlamingo relation vectors (all above 0.9) also raises the concern that the vectors may encode generic task/object priors rather than clean relation-specific knowledge.

The composite function-vector method has unresolved confounds. The weights are derived from source-example probabilities under each base vector, but there is little control for object identity, co-occurrence, or source-target relation matching. No ablation compares the learned weighting to fixed mixtures, single best base vectors, or other combination rules, even though the authors note that hand-crafted mixtures might perform better.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The code is said to be publicly available on GitHub, but no link is provided. Key details are missing or underspecified: exact AIE computation, top-head selection procedure, injection scaling/normalization, prompt templates, layer-selection protocol, model checkpoints, and random seeds. The GQA Agentic setup is also unclear: sampling '1,000 tasks per relation' from a training set with 707 images and 925 total relation instances implies substantial reuse or possible overlap, which should be clarified.

Some presentation and methodological details need improvement. There are numerous reference-year inconsistencies, the transfer experiment raises questions about applying synthetic-derived vectors (extracted at one layer) to GQA (evaluated at another layer), and the analogy-task construction and evaluation protocol are not described in enough detail to fully assess fairness against ICL baselines.
